lessons.title: Articles — Il, La, Lo, L'
lessons.explanation: Italian articles agree with the noun's gender and the first letter of the following word. Masculine: il (before consonant), lo (before s+consonant, z, ps, gn, x), l' (before vowel). Feminine: la (before consonant), l' (before vowel). Plural: i, gli, le.
examples: il libro (the book — masc.)
la casa (the house — fem.)
lo studente (the student — starts with st)
l'amico (the friend — starts with vowel)
gli amici (the friends — masc. pl. before vowel)
lessons.tip: The choice of article depends on the gender AND the first sound of the noun. Il → i (pl.); lo → gli (pl.); la → le (pl.).

quiz.question: Which article goes with 'studente' (student, masc., starts with 'st')?
Which article goes with 'amica' (female friend, starts with vowel)?

lessons.title: Essere and Stare — To Be
lessons.explanation: Like Spanish, Italian has two 'to be' verbs. Essere: permanent states, identity, origin, time, passive. Stare: health, location (sometimes), progressive tense (stare + gerundio). Essere is far more common.
examples: Sono italiano. (I am Italian.) — essere, identity
Come stai? (How are you?) — stare, health
Sto mangiando. (I am eating.) — stare + gerund
È tardi. (It is late.) — essere, time
lessons.tip: When in doubt, use essere. Stare is mainly for health ('come stai?') and the progressive form.

quiz.question: Which verb do you use for 'I am Italian' (identity)?
Which verb do you use for 'I am eating' (progressive)?

lessons.title: Present Tense — Regular Verbs
lessons.explanation: Italian verbs have three groups: -ARE, -ERE, -IRE. Drop the infinitive ending and add personal endings. -ARE (parlare): parlo, parli, parla, parliamo, parlate, parlano. -ERE (credere): credo, credi, crede, crediamo, credete, credono. -IRE (partire): parto, parti, parte, partiamo, partite, partono.
examples: Io parlo italiano. (I speak Italian.)
Tu credi in me. (You believe in me.)
Lei parte domani. (She leaves tomorrow.)
Noi mangiamo insieme. (We eat together.)
lessons.tip: Italian subject pronouns (io, tu, lui…) are usually omitted — the verb ending shows who is speaking.

lessons.title: Avere — To Have
lessons.explanation: The verb avere (to have): ho, hai, ha, abbiamo, avete, hanno. Used for possession and as an auxiliary for passato prossimo.
examples: Ho un gatto. (I have a cat.)
Hai fame? (Are you hungry?) — lit. do you have hunger?
Ha una macchina. (He/she has a car.)
Abbiamo tempo. (We have time.)
lessons.tip: Avere is used for many body sensations: avere fame (be hungry), avere sete (be thirsty), avere sonno (be sleepy), avere paura (be scared).

quiz.question: How do you say 'I have' in Italian?

lessons.title: Passato Prossimo — Recent Past
lessons.explanation: The passato prossimo is the main past tense. Use avere or essere + past participle. Verbs of motion, reflexives, and some state verbs use essere. With essere, the participle agrees in gender and number with the subject.
examples: Ho mangiato la pizza. (I ate pizza.) — avere
Sono andato/a al mercato. (I went to the market.) — essere
Abbiamo visto il film. (We saw the film.) — avere
Sono arrivati tardi. (They arrived late.) — essere, masc. pl.
lessons.tip: Verbs with essere: andare, venire, partire, arrivare, nascere, morire, stare, essere, rimanere, and all reflexive verbs.

quiz.question: Which auxiliary does 'andare' use in passato prossimo?

lessons.title: Congiuntivo — Subjunctive
lessons.explanation: The congiuntivo expresses doubt, wish, emotion, or uncertainty in subordinate clauses after 'che'. Present congiuntivo of -ARE verbs: parli, parli, parli, parliamo, parliate, parlino (note: io/tu/lui share same form).
examples: Voglio che tu venga. (I want you to come.)
È importante che studi. (It's important that you study.)
Penso che sia difficile. (I think it is difficult.)
Benché piova, usciamo. (Although it is raining, we go out.)
lessons.tip: The congiuntivo is triggered by expressions of desire, emotion, doubt, and impersonal expressions.

quiz.question: Which phrase triggers the Italian congiuntivo?

lessons.title: Periodo Ipotetico — Conditionals
lessons.explanation: Italian conditional sentences have three types. Real (possible): se + present → future. Unlikely: se + imperfetto congiuntivo → condizionale presente. Impossible (past): se + trapassato congiuntivo → condizionale passato.
examples: Se studio, prendo un bel voto. (If I study, I get a good grade.) — real
Se avessi tempo, verrei. (If I had time, I would come.) — unlikely
Se avessi studiato, avrei superato. (If I had studied, I would have passed.) — impossible
Se piove, resto a casa. (If it rains, I stay home.) — real
lessons.tip: Match the verb forms: real = present/future; unlikely = imperfect subj./conditional; impossible = past perfect subj./past conditional.

quiz.question: For an 'unlikely' Italian conditional, what tense goes in the 'se' clause?
